newsitem.title: USA: Intel promotes Grove, other executives.
newsitem.headline: Intel promotes Grove, other executives.

text.p: Intel Corp. Chief Executive Officer Andrew Grove will add the title of chairman May 21, and Chief Operating Officer Craig Barrett will also become president, the computer chip giant announced Monday.
Chairman Gordon Moore, the co-founder of Intel who is considered one of the fathers of the microprocessor industry, will become chairman emeritus in May.
"This series of moves is part of the ongoing management transition process at Intel," Moore said in a statement.

Grove's move from president to chairman and Barrett's from executive vice president to president have been expected to happen at some time. The three men have managed Intel together as the "executive office," and Intel said they will continue to do so.

"Craig is the guy who keeps the Intel machine running," Grove said of Barrett. "He is the architect of our manufacturing system and the principal driver behind our management methods and culture. In recent years I have shifted my activities to more of an industry focus; without Craig in place, this wouldn't have been possible."

Barrett, 57, has been executive vice president since 1990 and chief operating officer since 1993. He joined Intel in 1974 as technology development manager. He later ran Intel's manufacturing operations and managed the company's Microcomputer Components Group, which includes microprocessor products. He is a member of Intel's board of directors.
Grove, 60, who joined Intel at its founding in 1968 as head of research, has been its president since 1979 and chief executive officer since 1987.

Moore, 68, founded Intel with Robert Noyce in 1968 and has served as president and chief executive officer. He developed a theory in 1965 about the evolution of semiconductor chips -- that the amount of transistors that could be placed on a chip would double every 12 to 18 months. "Moore's Law" still holds true today.

Intel plans to report its earnings for the fourth quarter and for 1996 on Tuesday. Analysts on average estimate Intel earned $1.84 a share for the fourth quarter -- about double the 98 cents a share it earned in the same quarter a year earlier, according to First Call, which tracks analyst estimates. Intel's net income for the fourth quarter of last year was $867 million.
Analysts estimate Intel will earn $5.51 a share for 1996 vs. $3.94 a share for 1995, when it posted net income of $3.6 billion.
